newsitem.title: USA: EMU could hamper currency cooperation, study says.
newsitem.headline: EMU could hamper currency cooperation, study says.

text.p: The launch of European economic and monetary union will severely hamper international cooperation in currency markets and other areas if the EU does not change its policy-making institutions, a new study said.

The study, carried out for the Institute for International Economics by C. Randall Henning, urged the EU to decide who will represent the monetary union in international negotiations and organizations, and who will manage currency crises.

"American officials should insist on getting a clear answer to the question of who the Secretary of the Treasury telephones, or who telephones the Secretary, to address a crisis in the foreign exchange market," Henning said.
The study said that monetary union -- which it argues is probable, but not absolutely certain -- will pose a number of policy challenges for the United States.

Over the long term, the new European currency, the euro, will compete with the dollar for international status, the study said. In the short run, European countries that join monetary union will have an excess of dollar reserves.

Henning, an associate professor at American University, suggested that the monetary union use those excess reserves to capitalize a fund to provide financing to individual member countries facing economic difficulties.
Sales of dollars for that purpose would be coordinated with the United States and announced in advance.

"The United States and European monetary union should (also) counter currency stability by specifying a range of exchange rates beyond which fluctuations would be regarded as clearly not justified by the fundamentals," he added.
